newsitem.title: CHINA: China wants more investment funds in stock market.
newsitem.headline: China wants more investment funds in stock market.

text.p: China's decision to let three investment funds list on the Shanghai stock exchange, the first approval in three years, shows it wants more long-term funds and less speculation, brokers and fund managers said on Wednesday.

The three closed funds, totalling 300 million yuan ($36 million) and to be listed on Friday, were sold in 1993 to primary and secondary school teachers. They had thought that the funds would be listed, thereby making them tradeable.
But Beijing banned new fund listings, citing the lack of a developed market and proper regulations, leaving the teachers holding certificates that could not be transferred or traded.
"Beijing wants to channel more bank savings into investment funds," said Shao Jiejun, a manager at Shenyin Wanguo Securities which manages the Baoding Fund, one of the three to be listed.
"Personal bank savings are estimated to reach five trillion yuan at the end of this year," he said.
"The better off already have all they need for their daily life. Funds are an important investment channel for the stock market in addition to individual investment in stocks," he said.

A Chinese broker said the authorities want to reduce the short-term, speculative element in stock market trading often responsible for causing wide fluctuations in price, unrelated to the performance of the company.

"The market needs a wide variety of investment channels, including funds which take a longer term view than individuals, so we become nearer a situation where a company's performance determines its price," he said.
"I expect Beijing to approve more funds for listing next year, with the passing of regulations on investment funds due to be published late this year or early next year," he said.
The official press each day publishes prices of 22 funds listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, with the highest trading up to 6.10 yuan.
Shao said that Chinese investors had purchased investment funds with a total face value of six to seven billion yuan, some tradeable and some not.
His Baoding Fund was bought in the last quarter of 1993 by about 80,000 Shanghai teachers who have so far received only a single dividend of 0.18 yuan.
Its net asset value per unit reached 2.03 yuan as of September 30, 1996, up from its original one yuan. Shao estimated its trading price on Friday at about eight yuan.
Baoding has invested 15.91 percent of the fund into industrial projects and the rest in stocks, treasury bonds and cash.

But brokers said that, while the authorities wanted to develop the funds industry, a major obstacle remained turf battles in Beijing that have prevented the publication of a national securities law despite more than three years of debate.
The announcement of the listing of the three funds in Tuesday's newspaper said approval had been given by the People's Bank, the central bank, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange.
One broker said the People's Bank and the China Securities Regulatory Commission were struggling over the question of who should regulate the lucrative securities industry.
"In the case of investment funds, these two bodies are involved. But in the case of industrial funds, you have other ministries and government departments involved," a broker said.
